1: The weight of the Cloistered Emperor's word: whether an In-zen can pass beyond the Palace gates and be carried out across the realm.
3: The wealth of estates, proprietary provinces and the In's own domains, the Chōkōdō and Rengeō-in holdings among them.
5: The In's own soldiers: the Northern and Western Guard, and the warrior houses that can be summoned.
7: The hearts of court, country and the people of the capital.
9: Mastery of song, dance and refinement. It was the passion of the In's whole life, and it can move others too.
11: A name for scheming and guile. Every reversed In-zen and every two-faced bargain adds to it.
17: The Heike of Rokuhara: Kiyomori and his house.
18: The Kawachi Genji and the Minamoto of the provinces.
19: The Fujiwara regental house and the court nobility.
20: Enryaku-ji, Kōfuku-ji and the Kumano shrines.
21: The reigning Emperor and the close ministers of his personal rule.
26: Born in the age of cloistered rule, a fourth prince whom no one imagined could become emperor. Day and night, he cared for nothing but imayō.
31: Nine days after the In of Toba died, brothers, uncles and nephews, fathers and sons took up arms against one another. From then on began 「武者の世」 (“the age of warriors”). — after Jien, Gukanshō
36: Shinzei offered a scroll of the Song of Everlasting Sorrow as a warning; the In paid it no heed. On the night of the 9th day of the 12th month, Sanjō-dono went up in flames.
41: A thousand Kannon, one thousand and one images, the hall brimming with gold. A gift of the Heike, and the best years the two houses ever shared.
46: 「平氏」倒れ候ひぬ (“The Heishi has fallen”) — a wine flask topples over at Shunkan's villa in Shishigatani, in the Eastern Hills.
51: At fifty-three, the Cloistered Emperor is shut away in Toba-dono. Beyond the gate stand Kiyomori's soldiers; within it, there is only imayō.
56: The Heike flee west, the Rising-Sun General enters the capital, and the Cloistered Emperor's palace is burned. The realm is split three ways, and Kyoto's fields are strewn with the starved.
61: 「浪の下にも都のさぶらふぞ」 (“Beneath the waves, too, there is a capital.”) — the Nun of the Second Rank takes the child emperor in her arms and enters the sea.
66: A letter from Kamakura: the greatest tengu in Japan is none other than you.
71: If the soldiers of Rokuhara fell before an In-zen, whose realm would the realm then be?
74: Even after Kenshunmon-in, the Cloistered Emperor still sits face to face with Kiyomori. How much longer might the age of the Heike last?
77: The Cloistered Emperor goes west with the Heike; Kyoto and Yashima each serve an emperor of their own.
80: The fierce warrior of Kiso knows nothing of the capital's etiquette, but he knows who will live and die beside him.
83: With an In-zen in hand, the Hōgan need never brave the storm-tossed waves of Daimotsu-ura.
86: Beneath the Golden Hall of Hiraizumi, will the hundred and seventy thousand riders of Ōshū at last ride south?
90: The autumn rain has only just stopped, and the eaves of the Sanjō-Takakura mansion are still dripping. Taikenmon-in Shōshi has given birth to a son, and Emperor Toba names him *Masahito*. He is the fourth prince she has borne the Son of Heaven.
91: Everyone at court knows this child's arrival matters little. His eldest brother Akihito ascended the throne while still in swaddling clothes, as Emperor Sutoku; and the one who truly holds the realm is the Cloistered Emperor Shirakawa, past seventy, who says of himself: “The waters of the Kamo River, the dice of sugoroku, and the monks of the mountain — these alone I cannot bend to my will.” In the age of cloistered rule, the Emperor is only a doll seated behind the blinds; commands issue from the Retired Emperor's palace.
92: There is another whisper, passed behind the fans of the ladies-in-waiting: the In of Toba calls his eldest son Sutoku his “uncle-son,” claiming he is truly the seed of the Cloistered Emperor Shirakawa. You are still in the arms of your nurse, Lady Kii, and cannot understand such things. But thirty years from now, those words will become the flames soaring over Shirakawa-kita-dono.
93: In Daiji 4, the Cloistered Emperor Shirakawa dies, and the In of Toba begins his cloistered rule. As you grow, you find that what you love most is not the Chinese classics, nor the bow and horse, but the popular songs passed from the lips of puppeteer women, shirabyōshi dancers and courtesans — *imayō*.
94: Emperor Go-Shirakawa, personal name Masahito, was the fourth son of Emperor Toba; his mother was Taikenmon-in Fujiwara no Shōshi. The “uncle-son” story appears in the Kojidan; most scholars regard it as rumor not to be wholly trusted.
95: Cloistered Emperor Shirakawa's “three things in the realm beyond my will” is found in The Tale of the Heike, Book One.
96: Sing imayō day and night, seeking out puppeteer women and courtesans as teachers
97: You entered this path as a boy, never noticing the eastern sky grow pale
98: Study the Records of the Grand Historian and the Essentials of Government of the Zhenguan Era with scholars
99: Though not the heir, you should still know what makes order and chaos
100: Befriend the young men of the Ise Taira in the Northern Guard
101: Kiyomori, son of Taira no Tadamori, is nine years your senior
102: Accompany your mother on pilgrimage to the Three Shrines of Kumano
103: In Kumano's three thousand six hundred peaks, gods and buddhas dwell together
107: Over these years, your mother's radiance has been stripped away bit by bit. The In of Toba dotes on the newly arrived Fujiwara no Tokushi, raising her as Bifukumon-in; in Eiji 1, your eldest brother Sutoku is forced to abdicate in favor of her three-year-old son, who becomes *Emperor Konoe*. The abdication edict names the boy “Crown Brother” rather than “Crown Prince,” so Sutoku can never rule as the Emperor's father from the cloister. Your mother soon takes the tonsure and withdraws to the Hōkongō-in at Ninna-ji.
108: You have a family of your own now. Yoshiko, adopted daughter of Minamoto no Arihito, bore you a son, *Morihito*, but died soon after the birth. Morihito was taken as Bifukumon-in's adopted son and carried off to another palace.
109: In the 8th month of Kyūan 1, your mother falls gravely ill. You keep watch by her bed for several nights, watching her hand grow ever lighter. After she draws her last breath, you sing imayō before her bier, one song after another, singing on when your voice is gone, until your throat bleeds. Later you will write in the Kudenshū of the Ryōjin Hishō: three times in my youth I lost my voice, for I sang day and night without ceasing.
110: “Prince Masahito, is it…” The noble hides his mouth behind his fan. “He sings well enough. A pity he is not the stuff of which emperors are made.”
111: Taikenmon-in died in Kyūan 1 (1145). Go-Shirakawa's own account of his devotion to imayō and of losing his voice three times appears in the Kudenshū of the Ryōjin Hishō, Book Ten.
112: That Emperor Konoe's accession edict called him “Crown Brother” is recorded in the Gukanshō; this was the beginning of Sutoku's resentment.
113: Sing through the night, sending your mother off with imayō
114: It is the only rite you know
115: Draw close to Bifukumon-in and visit Morihito often
116: The child is your flesh and blood, and Bifukumon-in's bargaining chip
117: Grieve alongside your brother Sutoku, visiting his palace often
118: Born of the same mother, slighted alike
121: The Tengu Image of Mount Atago
122: On the 23rd day of the 7th month of Kyūju 2, Emperor Konoe dies at Konoe-dono, only seventeen and without an heir.
123: Rumors at once sweep the capital: someone has found iron nails driven into the eyes of the tengu image on Mount Atago. A shrine maiden, possessed by the god, declares that the Emperor's eye ailment and death were the work of a curse — and that the ones who cast it were the Minister of the Left, *Fujiwara no Yorinaga*, and his father Tadazane. Bifukumon-in believes it without a doubt, and from then on the In of Toba holds Yorinaga at arm's length.
124: Who should have the throne? The Retired Emperor Sutoku hopes his son, *Prince Shigehito*, will succeed, so that he himself may rule from the cloister. Bifukumon-in will never allow it. She confers in secret with the Chancellor *Fujiwara no Tadamichi* and the lay priest *Shinzei*: the most fitting choice is her adopted son Morihito — but Morihito's father still lives, and the son cannot be raised over the father.
125: And so you, twenty-nine years old and singing all day long, are chosen. Shinzei is the husband of your nurse, Lady Kii, and he counsels the In of Toba: enthrone Masahito as a stopgap, and pass the throne to Morihito once he is grown. The Emperor, in other words, is only temporary.
126: “By decree of the In of Toba: Prince Masahito is to ascend the throne this very day.”
128: “Your Highness need not trouble yourself. We ask only that you sit upon the throne for a while. When Prince Morihito is grown, Your Highness may return to song and dance.”
129: “Then how many years does the lay priest think I shall sit there?”
130: “That depends — on how many years Your Highness wishes to sit.”
131: You hear the cicadas in the garden, and suddenly they sound like the rhythm of an imayō.
132: Emperor Konoe's death and the tale of nails in the eyes of the Atago tengu image are found in the Taiki and the Gukanshō.
133: Go-Shirakawa's accession as a “stopgap” was settled by Bifukumon-in, Tadamichi and Shinzei. Shinzei's (Fujiwara no Michinori's) wife, Fujiwara no Asako, was Go-Shirakawa's nurse.
134: Accept humbly and ascend the throne
136: Decline three times before accepting, so court and country know you do not covet the throne
137: For the first time, you taste the art of refusal
138: Petition openly for Sutoku's son Shigehito to inherit the line
139: Bifukumon-in will never agree, but your brother will remember
140: Refuse the throne, flee to Eguchi and sing with the courtesans
141: From now on, the realm is nothing to you
145: On the day of the enthronement, the banners before the Daigokuden snap in the wind. You put on the crown and take the high throne. Below, the hundred officials bow and dance; you are counting the wind-bells at the corners of the eaves — and at the seventh, the ceremony ends.
146: You make Kinshi, daughter of Fujiwara no Kinyoshi, your empress. The Emperor's days are one ceremony after another. The real edicts still come from the In of Toba; your name appears only at the head of the proclamations.
147: Lady Kii whispers to you: “The lay priest Shinzei says that if the Emperor has leisure, he might do well to read more.” You smile, and that night summon the imayō singers as always.
148: “Your Majesty,” Lady Kii murmurs as she straightens your collar, “the In of Toba coughed blood again today.”
149: The whole capital is waiting for a single moment.
150: Go-Shirakawa was enthroned on the 26th day of the 10th month of Kyūju 2, and made Fujiwara no Kinshi his empress.
151: Cultivate Shinzei in secret and learn his stratagems
152: He is your nurse's husband, and the cleverest man in the capital
153: Carry on with music every night
154: Why take a stopgap reign seriously?
155: Send envoys to inquire after your ailing father
156: Filial devotion may buy a little trust
160: On the 2nd day of the 7th month of Hōgen 1, the Cloistered Emperor Toba dies, aged fifty-four.
161: Before the end, the Retired Emperor Sutoku hurries to Toba Tanaka-dono, begging to see his father one last time. But the gate is shut. It is guarded by your own close retainers, who say only: by the Cloistered Emperor's final command, he is not to be admitted.
162: Your brother stands outside the gate a long while. You remember how, when your mother lay ill, the two of you sat side by side in the corridors of the Hōkongō-in.
163: Inside the hall, through layer upon layer of blinds, you seem to hear your brother's footsteps beyond the gate.
164: Some days earlier, the In of Toba had already ordered Minamoto no Yoshitomo, Minamoto no Yoshiyasu and other warriors to guard Takamatsu-dono and Toba-dono. Everything was arranged; all that remained was for the last breath to fail.
165: “Masahito! It's me! Let me see Father — just once!”
166: “I am Father's eldest son! Who dares bar my way?”
167: “Your Majesty, if the Retired Emperor enters, the Minister of the Left (Yorinaga) will surely use it to stir up trouble. The Cloistered Emperor's final command must not be defied.”
168: The Cloistered Emperor Toba died on the 2nd day of the 7th month of Hōgen 1. Sutoku's failure to gain entry to see his father is recorded in the Hōgen Monogatari and the Hyōhanki.
169: Obey your father's final command and keep your brother out
170: The historical path. Sutoku leaves in fury
171: Open the doors yourself and let your brother in to say farewell
172: Shinzei will be displeased, but your brother will remember this moment
173: Hōgen 1 (1156), 7th month, night of the 10th day
176: Eight days after the In of Toba's death, the Retired Emperor Sutoku moves to Shirakawa-kita-dono, and the Minister of the Left Yorinaga comes up to the capital from Uji. The former police commissioner Minamoto no Tameyoshi, his son *Chinzei Hachirō Tametomo*, and Taira no Tadamasa all gather at the northern palace.
177: On your side, Takamatsu-dono blazes with lamplight. The Chancellor Tadamichi sits on the left, Shinzei on the right; in the courtyard stand two warrior chiefs — *Taira no Kiyomori* of the Ise Taira and *Minamoto no Yoshitomo* of the Kawachi Genji. Yoshitomo's father Tameyoshi and brother Tametomo are in the opposing camp.
178: “The essence of war is to strike first. Tonight, while they are unprepared, let us fall upon Shirakawa-kita-dono by night — it will surely be broken before dawn!”
179: “A night attack… that is the way of bandits. How can it be the way the court punishes rebels?”
180: “The Chancellor speaks of the courtesies of peace. This is not a time of peace. Yoshitomo is right.”
181: Only later did people learn that at that same hour, Tametomo in Shirakawa-kita-dono had proposed a night attack as well, only to be overruled by Yorinaga: “That is the method of private feuds, not of the court's army.”
182: Everything hangs on a single word from you.
183: The forces on each side in the Hōgen Disturbance and the debate over the night attack are found in the Hōgen Monogatari, the Hyōhanki and the Gukanshō. Yorinaga's rejection of Tametomo's night-attack plan is recorded in the Hōgen Monogatari.
184: Approve Yoshitomo's plan: march at the hour of the Tiger tonight
185: No night attack; wait for dawn and strike in open array
186: Do you have the strength to absorb their first blow?
187: Send an envoy to Shirakawa-kita-dono to make peace with your brother
188: Requires your brother to still hold some affection for you
189: You grieved with Sutoku, or opened the doors for his farewell
190: Hōgen 1 (1156), 7th month, 11th day, hour of the Tiger
192: Before dawn, Kiyomori's three hundred riders, Yoshitomo's two hundred and Yoshiyasu's hundred cross the Kamo River and advance east.
193: The western gate of Shirakawa-kita-dono is held by Chinzei Hachirō Tametomo alone. He stands seven feet tall, his left arm four inches longer than his right, and his bow takes five men to string. A single arrow pierces two horsemen. Kiyomori's retainers fall in heaps before the gate, and Kiyomori is forced to try another. Yoshitomo charges the western gate himself; Tametomo's arrow strikes the star from Yoshitomo's helmet — he is his brother, and Tametomo stays his hand.
194: By the hour of the Dragon, Yoshitomo asks the In's leave to set fire to it. The northern palace goes up in flames, the blaze reddening the sky over all Shirakawa. The Retired Emperor Sutoku escapes through the fire and flees to Nyoigatake; Yorinaga, struck in the neck by a stray arrow, makes his way to Nara to seek his father Tadazane. Tadazane shuts his gate and will not receive him. Three days later, Yorinaga breathes his last.
195: “I report to Your Majesty: Shirakawa-kita-dono has fallen, the Retired Emperor has fled, and the Minister of the Left has been struck by an arrow.” There is still ash on his armor.
196: Your fingers feel ice-cold. Jien would later write in the Gukanshō that from this day on, “Japan” became 「武者の世」 (“the age of warriors”).
197: The course of the Hōgen Disturbance follows the Hōgen Monogatari and the Hyōhanki. The description of Tametomo's prowess comes from the Hōgen Monogatari and may be exaggerated. The phrase 「武者の世」 (“the age of warriors”) is from the Gukanshō, Book Four.
202: You resolve to wait for dawn. But Tametomo in Shirakawa-kita-dono does not wait for Yorinaga's leave: at the hour of the Ox, he leads twenty-eight riders in a surprise attack on the eastern gate of Takamatsu-dono.
203: Fire arrows land on the roof of your sleeping hall. Ladies-in-waiting flee screaming, and the Northern Guard grapple with the enemy in the dark. Yoshitomo brings his men back to the rescue and fights his own brother before the gate.
204: Only at daybreak does your side steady its lines, march east and burn Shirakawa-kita-dono. Sutoku flees; Yorinaga dies of an arrow wound. You have won — but half of Takamatsu-dono is burned, your Northern Guard lie dead and wounded in disarray, and the whole capital is saying that the Emperor nearly lost his life to an eighteen-year-old warrior.
205: For the first time you understand: what those samurai hold in their hands is more direct than any proclamation.
206: This is an imagined line. Historically, Tametomo's night-attack plan was rejected by Yorinaga and never carried out.
207: Clear away the wreckage and judge the guilty
210: Your envoy reaches Shirakawa-kita-dono. The Retired Emperor Sutoku reads your letter and falls silent for a long time. But Yorinaga, at his side, sneers: “The Emperor sends a sheet of paper and expects the Retired Emperor to lay down his arms?”
211: The envoy returns empty-handed. Yoshitomo is already impatient, and Shinzei counsels: “Your Majesty has done all a heart can do. If he will not accept, the wrong is his.”
212: At the hour of the Tiger, the troops march.
215: You send no envoy. You shed the Emperor's robes, wear only a hunting cloak, and with a dozen riders knock at the gate of Shirakawa-kita-dono by night.
216: Tametomo stands on the gate tower, bow in hand, and freezes when he sees the Emperor himself. The Retired Emperor Sutoku runs out barefoot. The two brothers face each other beneath the torches, and neither speaks first.
217: “Brother,” you say at last, “if Mother were alive, she would never wish to see us take up arms against each other.”
218: “Masahito… do you know, I have waited fifteen years to hear those words.”
219: Sutoku weeps. He agrees to disband the troops at the northern palace and take the tonsure at Ninna-ji; Yorinaga refuses and flees toward Nara with his followers, but falls from his horse on the way and dies of his injuries. Yoshitomo persuades his father Tameyoshi and brother Tametomo to surrender. Not a single arrow is loosed at Shirakawa-kita-dono.
220: Shinzei waits at Takamatsu-dono until dawn; seeing you return, he only sighs: “This is something your servant could never have foreseen.” Yoshitomo and Kiyomori, however, exchange glances — the blades they had sharpened went unused.
221: This is an imagined line. Historically, the two sides fought on the 11th day of the 7th month; Sutoku was captured and exiled to Sanuki.
225: The disturbance is quelled. The Retired Emperor Sutoku shaves his head at Ninna-ji and begs forgiveness. Tameyoshi, Tadamasa and the rest surrender.
226: Shinzei drafts the sentences: Sutoku to be exiled to Sanuki; Tameyoshi, Tadamasa and their sons to be *beheaded*.
227: The nobles are aghast. Since the Kusuko Incident of the Kōnin era, the court has not carried out an execution in more than three hundred and forty years.
228: Yet Shinzei says: “If we do not behead them, there will be rebellion again.” More dreadful still, he wants Yoshitomo to behead his own father Tameyoshi, and Kiyomori his own uncle Tadamasa.
229: “Your servant… would trade every reward for the Hōgen battle for my father Tameyoshi's life.” Yoshitomo kneels in the courtyard, his brow pressed to the white sand.
230: “Captain of the Left Stables, the law of the court cannot be set aside for one man's filial piety.”
231: The revival of the death penalty after the Hōgen Disturbance is recorded in the Gukanshō and the Hōgen Monogatari. Tameyoshi was beheaded by his son Yoshitomo at Funaokayama; Tadamasa was beheaded by Kiyomori.
232: The Retired Emperor Sutoku was exiled to Sanuki and never returned to the capital.
233: Follow Shinzei's counsel: behead the commanders and exile your brother to Sanuki
234: Spare Tameyoshi alone and exile him; your brother is still exiled to Sanuki
235: Yoshitomo will never forget this mercy
236: Pardon all death sentences; confine your brother at Ninna-ji
237: A name for clemency, but Shinzei will say you are raising a tiger to devour you
241: Rewards are handed out according to merit. Kiyomori receives the governorship of Harima, a rich province; Yoshitomo gets only the post of Acting Captain of the Right Stables, and only after pressing again and again is he made Captain of the Left Stables.
242: As he withdraws, Yoshitomo looks back once at Kiyomori's retreating figure.
243: Shinzei presides over everything. He drafts the Hōgen New Ordinances, proclaiming: “The lands of the nine provinces belong to one man alone; beyond the royal command, what private authority may be wielded?” All land in the realm belongs to the Emperor, and every estate must have its deeds. He rebuilds the Greater Palace and revives the long-lapsed sumō festival and the inner banquet. People in the capital say it is a splendor unseen since the reigns of Engi and Tenryaku.
